`ResponsesAgent` is the recommended MLflow interface for production agents. Its documented benefits include:
- **Advanced agent capabilities**: multi-agent support, streaming output, a comprehensive tool-calling message history (several messages including intermediate tool calls), tool-calling confirmation and long-running tools.
- **Streamlined development and deployment**: any framework can be wrapped, typed Python classes help the IDE, MLflow infers the signature automatically, `predict` and `predict_stream` are traced automatically, and AI Gateway inference tables (now under Unity Gateway) are enabled for deployed agents.
## What it does not do
It does not replace dependency declaration: resources an agent needs at serving time are still declared with the `resources` argument at logging time so that credentials can be provisioned.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Message history and streaming (correct):** the interface returns multiple messages, including intermediate tool-calling messages, and supports streamed output in smaller chunks.
- ✗ **B. No resource declaration:** resources are still declared at logging time for automatic authentication passthrough.
- ✗ **C. Only LangGraph:** any third-party framework can be used; the agent is wrapped, not rewritten in one specific library.
- ✗ **D. Legacy schema only:** the schema is compatible with the OpenAI Responses schema, and the ChatCompletion-style interfaces are the older ones.
- ✓ **E. Automatic signature inference (correct):** MLflow produces a valid signature for a `ResponsesAgent` when it is logged, so the manual signature step can be skipped.

## Key idea
`ResponsesAgent` adds automatic signatures, tool-call history and streaming to any framework.
Q012285:
## Evaluation versus monitoring
Agent quality is a loop. **Evaluation** happens before release: you run scorers (LLM judges and code-based checks) over a fixed, curated dataset with `mlflow.genai.evaluate()` and compare app versions on the same inputs, so any difference comes from the change and not from different traffic. **Monitoring** happens after release: the same scorers run on traces from real traffic.
## Which fits the question
Choosing between two candidates before launch is a controlled comparison, which is evaluation. The dataset with reference answers also lets ground-truth judges such as `Correctness` run.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Data profiling:** profiling tracks data tables and tables of model inputs and outputs, and does not rank two prompt versions by answer quality.
- ✗ **B. Live traffic split:** this exposes real users to the weaker prompt, and traffic differs between the groups, so it is not a controlled comparison before release.
- ✗ **C. Reading a few traces:** tracing is essential for debugging, but a handful of hand-picked traces is neither systematic nor repeatable.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Evaluation scores each version on the same curated inputs with the same scorers, so the comparison is repeatable and needs no real users.

## Key idea
Evaluation compares versions on a fixed dataset before release.
Q012286:
## Why evaluation is not enough
An evaluation dataset is a snapshot of the questions you expected at release. Real traffic shifts: new products, new phrasing, new failure modes. A fixed dataset cannot show that.
## Monitoring in the quality loop
The quality loop continues after release: **monitor production by running scorers against live traffic**, so that a regression is caught and the next issue can be fixed. In practice this means tracing the deployed agent and scoring a configurable sample of its traces. Sampling trades coverage against compute cost. Note that production monitoring of agents is documented as a Beta feature at the time of writing, so check the status before relying on it; the concept (score live traces with the same scorers) is what the exam objective tests.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Scoring a sample of live traces with the same scorers measures quality on real, changing traffic, so the drop on the new product line is seen without waiting for complaints.
- ✗ **B. Nightly re-run of the fixed set:** the dataset has no questions about the new product line, so it keeps passing while real quality falls.
- ✗ **C. Turning tracing off:** traces are the data scorers read; removing them leaves no evidence about production quality.
- ✗ **D. Larger top-k:** more retrieved chunks may or may not help and cannot be called a prevention; without measuring, you do not know whether quality recovered.

## Key idea
Monitoring scores sampled live traces to catch drift that a fixed evaluation set cannot see.
Q012287:
## Cost and coverage in monitoring
Monitoring runs scorers (LLM judges or code checks) on traces from real traffic. Each LLM-judge call costs compute, so scoring every trace on a busy agent is expensive. The scorer has a **sampling rate**, the fraction of traces it evaluates, which trades coverage against cost: a lower rate is cheaper but can miss rare failures, a higher rate sees more but costs more.
## Status note
Production monitoring of agents is documented as Beta at the time of writing. The idea tested here, sampling live traces with the same scorers used in evaluation, is the concept from the quality loop; re-check the feature status before relying on it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Evaluation dataset per request:** the curated set is a fixed pre-release snapshot and does not measure the real questions users ask.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** A lower sampling rate scores fewer traces, so judge cost drops while a representative sample of real traffic still shows how quality moves.
- ✗ **C. One request a day:** a sample that small cannot represent daily traffic and would miss most regressions.
- ✗ **D. No traces:** scorers read traces, so removing them ends production quality measurement instead of reducing its cost.

## Key idea
Tune the scorer sampling rate to trade monitoring coverage against judge cost.
Q012288:
## Closing the loop between monitoring and evaluation
The quality loop in Databricks MLflow guidance is: trace the agent, find an issue, collect feedback and curate a dataset, write a scorer, fix the agent, evaluate the fix, and monitor production again. Production traces that fail are the best raw material for evaluation data because they are real examples of the issue.
Production monitoring of agents is documented as Beta at the time of writing, so re-check its status; the loop itself (turn failed traces into evaluation data, re-evaluate) uses GA evaluation.
## What the team should do
Review the flagged traces, add representative failures (with the correct expected facts) and known-good examples to an evaluation dataset, then run the evaluation on the new and previous versions. The fix is confirmed on the failure cases, and the rest of the dataset shows that nothing else regressed.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Steering users:** hiding a topic is not a fix and hurts the product.
- ✗ **B. Delete traces:** removing evidence does not change agent behavior, and the score would stay low for new questions.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Failed traces become regression test cases, so the evaluation proves the fix and guards other topics, and monitoring then keeps watching.
- ✗ **D. Lower sampling:** this reports fewer problems, but the answers stay wrong; sampling controls coverage and cost, not quality.

## Key idea
Turn failing production traces into evaluation data and re-evaluate the fix.
Q012289:
## Two phases, one set of scorers
- **Evaluation** (development): `mlflow.genai.evaluate()` runs scorers over an evaluation dataset against an app version. Inputs are fixed, so versions are comparable and experiments are repeatable. Expected answers allow ground-truth judges.
- **Monitoring** (production): scorers run automatically on a sample of production traces, which shows how quality moves as real traffic changes. A sampling rate balances coverage against compute cost. Results are attached to traces as feedback.
Databricks documents the same scorers for both phases, so a judge written for evaluation can be moved to monitoring. Production monitoring of agents is documented as Beta today, so treat the feature status as something to re-check.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Separate scorers:** the same scorers can be reused in both phases, which keeps measurement consistent.
- ✗ **B. Reference per request:** live traffic has no expected answers, so monitoring uses reference-free judges.
- ✓ **C. Evaluation on a dataset (correct):** a fixed curated dataset makes version comparison repeatable and allows expected answers.
- ✗ **D. Reversed phases:** evaluation is the controlled, pre-release comparison, and monitoring is the one that watches live traffic.
- ✓ **E. Monitoring on live traces (correct):** scorers on sampled real traces show quality changes in production.

## Key idea
Evaluate on a fixed dataset before release; monitor sampled live traces after.
Q012290:
## Genie Agents API
Genie Agents (formerly called Genie spaces) can be integrated into your own chatbot, agent or application through the Genie Agents API. It has three groups of capabilities:
- **Chat mode APIs**: natural-language data querying in applications and agent frameworks. They support stateful conversations, where users ask follow-up questions and explore data over time.
- **Agent mode APIs**: send prompts in Agent mode, stream reasoning and SQL results and receive final reports with citations.
- **Management APIs**: create, configure and deploy Genie Agents across workspaces, for CI/CD and version control.
## Why stateful chat
The follow-up "Now only for EMEA" is ambiguous without the earlier question. A conversation in Chat mode holds the history, so Genie resolves the reference itself.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Chat mode conversations are stateful, so the second question is interpreted with the first, and the supervisor does not manage context by hand.
- ✗ **B. New agent per turn:** an agent is a configured data context (tables, instructions, examples), not a conversation, and creating one per turn loses history and is wasteful.
- ✗ **C. One-off requests with pasted context:** this rebuilds by hand what a Chat mode conversation already stores and risks wrong or truncated context.
- ✗ **D. Regex on cached SQL:** this bypasses Genie's understanding of the data and breaks as soon as the question is phrased differently.

## Key idea
Use Chat mode conversations for stateful follow-ups with a Genie Agent.
Q012291:
## Asynchronous messages in the Genie Agents API
Chat mode messages are processed asynchronously: the client sends a message and then reads its status until a conclusive state is reached. The Databricks best practices for the Genie API are:
- Poll for status updates every 1 to 5 seconds until a conclusive status such as `COMPLETED`, `FAILED` or `CANCELLED`, and limit polling to 10 minutes for most queries; after that, stop and return a timeout error.
- Use exponential backoff for polling, increasing the delay up to a maximum of one minute.
- Add your own retry logic with exponential backoff, because the API does not retry failed requests for you.
- Start a new conversation for each session; reusing threads across sessions can reduce accuracy.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Resending the message:** this creates new messages and new work for Genie each time; the documented approach is to poll the one message that was sent.
- ✗ **B. Fixed wait:** duration depends on the question, so a fixed delay wastes time on fast queries and still misses slow ones.
- ✗ **C. Open connection:** results are read by polling the message status, not by holding a connection until the answer is written.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Polling the message status with growing delays gets the result as soon as it is ready, keeps the request rate low and ends cleanly on failure or timeout.

## Key idea
Poll the Genie message status with exponential backoff until a conclusive state or a timeout.
Q012292:
## Resources and automatic authentication passthrough
A deployed agent runs on a serving endpoint, not as the notebook user. For Databricks-managed resources, the agent declares its dependencies at logging time with the `resources` parameter (for a Genie Agent the resource class is `DatabricksGenieSpace`, named after Genie spaces). At deployment Databricks checks that the endpoint creator can access every declared dependency, creates a service principal for the agent model version, grants it access, and injects short-lived credentials that it rotates.
## Permission needed
For a Genie Agent the endpoint creator needs `CAN RUN`. Other supported resources have their own permission, for example `Can Use` on an AI Search index and `EXECUTE` on a Unity Catalog function. A resource that was never declared gets no such credential, so the call fails.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Hard-coded personal token:** a long-lived credential in code is the manual method with the highest risk, and the automatic passthrough was designed to avoid it.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Declaring the Genie Agent at logging time lets Databricks provision credentials for it, and the creator's CAN RUN is what allows that access to be granted.
- ✗ **C. Share with everybody:** this widens access for all users to fix one service, and the endpoint still would not hold a declared, managed credential.
- ✗ **D. Embed Genie in the container:** Genie Agents are workspace objects; they are reached through the API, not packaged into an image.

## Key idea
Declare Genie Agents (and other resources) when logging so the endpoint gets managed credentials.
Q012293:
## Three groups of Genie API capabilities
- **Chat mode APIs**: stateful natural-language data querying with follow-up questions and history.
- **Agent mode APIs**: send prompts in Agent mode, stream the reasoning and SQL results, and receive final reports with citations.
- **Management APIs**: programmatic creation, configuration and deployment of Genie Agents across workspaces, for CI/CD pipelines, version control and automated management.
## Creating an agent in code
The Create Genie Agent API (`POST /api/2.0/genie/spaces`) takes a title, a SQL warehouse and a serialized definition (`serialized_space`) that holds the tables, instructions, example SQL, join specs and SQL snippets, so one reviewed definition can be applied to many workspaces. Creating or updating needs CAN USE on a pro or serverless SQL warehouse and SELECT on the data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. UI only:** agents can be created and updated programmatically through the Create Genie Agent API.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** The Management APIs exist for CI/CD and cross-workspace deployment, so a pipeline can apply one reviewed definition to every production workspace.
- ✗ **C. Chat mode:** these APIs run conversations against an existing agent and do not copy its configuration anywhere.
- ✗ **D. Agent mode:** they return reasoning, SQL and cited reports for prompts, not a deployable copy of the configuration.

## Key idea
Use the Genie Management APIs to deploy agents across workspaces in CI/CD.
Q012294:
## Chat mode versus Agent mode
- **Chat mode APIs**: stateful conversations in which users ask follow-up questions; you retrieve the generated SQL, query results and visualizations.
- **Agent mode APIs**: send prompts in Agent mode, stream the reasoning and SQL results while they are produced, and receive a final report with citations.
Both need at least CAN VIEW on the Genie Agent and SELECT on the data it uses, and data access is evaluated with the caller's own Unity Catalog permissions.
## Choosing
A short follow-up question inside a conversation suits Chat mode. A deeper investigation whose progress and cited conclusion the application wants to show suits Agent mode.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Agent mode is the documented way to stream reasoning and SQL results and to receive a final report with citations.
- ✗ **B. Query history:** the Agent mode API streams the reasoning and results to the caller directly.
- ✗ **C. Chat mode:** it returns SQL, results and visualizations for conversational follow-ups; streamed reasoning and cited reports belong to Agent mode.
- ✗ **D. Management APIs:** they create and deploy agents and do not answer prompts.

## Key idea
Use Agent mode APIs for streamed reasoning and cited reports; use Chat mode for follow-ups.
Q012295:
## Custom pyfunc models
MLflow's Python function (`pyfunc`) flavor lets you deploy any piece of Python code or Python model. Typical reasons are: the model needs preprocessing before its predict function, the framework is not natively supported by MLflow, the raw output needs post-processing, the model has per-request branching logic, or you are deploying fully custom code.
## The two required functions
- `load_context`: anything that must be loaded only once, such as weights or a tokenizer.
- `predict`: all logic that runs for every request. Here you format inputs, call the model and format outputs.
Logging this class gives one artifact and one endpoint that contains the whole chain.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Pull at request time:** this adds latency and a runtime dependency, and the logged model no longer captures what ran.
- ✗ **B. Clients repeat the logic:** duplicated preprocessing in many apps drifts and breaks consistency between training and serving.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** A pyfunc class holds preprocessing, model call and post-processing in `predict`, so one served artifact returns the final label with its confidence.
- ✗ **D. Second endpoint:** two network hops, two things to deploy and version, and clients must orchestrate the sequence themselves.

## Key idea
Put pre- and post-processing inside a custom pyfunc model's `predict`.
Q012296:
## Parameters without code changes
Agent code often has values that change between environments: the model endpoint name, prompt text, retriever settings. MLflow `ModelConfig` is a set of key-value parameters you define in a Python dictionary or a `.yaml` file. In the agent code you create `mlflow.models.ModelConfig(development_config=...)` and read values with `model_config.get("name")` (or convert with `to_dict()`). When you log the agent you pass the `model_config` parameter to `log_model`, which sets the parameters used when the logged agent is loaded.
## Why it helps
During development you can use a dictionary, then move to a YAML file for production and CI/CD. The code file stays the same, and the logged model records the parameters it was built with.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Notebook environment variables:** the logged model does not capture notebook session variables, so the endpoint would not see them.
- ✗ **B. Git pull at request time:** this adds latency and a runtime dependency, and the logged model no longer records what ran.
- ✗ **C. Copies per environment:** duplicated code drifts and every change needs edits in several places.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** `ModelConfig` separates parameters from code, and the `model_config` argument to `log_model` fixes the values the logged agent will use.

## Key idea
Use `ModelConfig` and the `model_config` argument of `log_model` to change agent parameters without editing code.
Q012297:
## Files needed at inference time
When a model needs files during inference, package them into the model artifact when you log it. With `mlflow.pyfunc.log_model` you pass the `artifacts` parameter, a dictionary that maps names to paths (for example files in a Unity Catalog volume or a local directory). In a pyfunc model the paths are then available from the `context` object under `context.artifacts`, and you load them in `load_context` the usual way for that file type.
## Why
A serving endpoint runs in its own container. The notebook driver's disk does not exist there, and downloading files from the internet at startup can fail or be blocked. Packaging files with the model makes the logged version self-contained.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. `pip_requirements`:** it lists Python packages to install, not data files such as weights or templates.
- ✗ **B. Driver local disk:** the endpoint runs in a separate container that does not share the notebook driver's disk, so those paths do not exist.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** The `artifacts` argument bundles the files with the logged model, and `context.artifacts` gives `load_context` their paths inside the serving container.
- ✗ **D. Files from clients:** this sends large content on every call, duplicates it in many apps and is not part of the logged model.

## Key idea
Package inference-time files with the `artifacts` argument and read them through `context.artifacts`.
Q012298:
## When to reach for pyfunc
The Databricks guide lists these scenarios for a custom Python function model: the model requires preprocessing before inputs reach its predict function; the framework is not natively supported by MLflow; the application requires the model's raw outputs to be post-processed; the model has per-request branching logic; or you are deploying fully custom code.
## What pyfunc does not change
A pyfunc model is still logged with its dependencies, registered in Unity Catalog and served like any other model. A natively supported flavor that needs no extra logic does not need the wrapper.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Skip registration:** pyfunc models are registered and served like others and the registry step stays.
- ✓ **B. Preprocessing (correct):** input cleaning before `predict` is a documented pyfunc scenario.
- ✗ **C. Unmodified standard model:** a native flavor can be logged and served without a wrapper.
- ✗ **D. No dependencies:** pyfunc logs requirements, and `pip_requirements` is how you control them.
- ✓ **E. Post-processing (correct):** reshaping raw outputs for the consumer is the other documented scenario.

## Key idea
Use pyfunc for pre- and post-processing, unsupported frameworks and custom branching logic.
Q012299:
## Serving endpoint permission levels
A serving endpoint has an ACL with four levels, in increasing power:
- **No permissions**: nothing.
- **CAN VIEW**: get the endpoint and list endpoints.
- **CAN QUERY**: everything CAN VIEW allows, plus querying the endpoint.
- **CAN MANAGE**: everything above plus updating the endpoint configuration, deleting it and modifying its permissions.
## Least privilege
A client application that only sends requests needs CAN QUERY. CAN MANAGE belongs to the owners who change or delete the endpoint. CAN VIEW alone is not enough to query.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** CAN QUERY allows requests to the endpoint and nothing that changes it, which matches least privilege for a calling application.
- ✗ **B. CAN MANAGE:** it would let the application update, delete or re-permission the endpoint, exactly what security forbids.
- ✗ **C. CAN VIEW:** it only allows getting and listing the endpoint; querying requires CAN QUERY.
- ✗ **D. No permission:** with no permission a principal cannot query; access is granted through the ACL.

## Key idea
Give calling apps CAN QUERY on a serving endpoint, and keep CAN MANAGE for owners.
Q012300:
## Authentication choices for deployed agents
- **Automatic authentication passthrough**: the agent runs with the permissions of the user who deployed it, through credentials Databricks manages. You declare dependencies at logging time. Low setup, short-lived credentials, automatic rotation. Recommended when all resources support it.
- **Manual authentication**: you provide credentials, for example in environment variables. These are long-lived and need rotation management.
- On-behalf-of-user authentication runs as the end user, which is for per-user access control or user-attributed auditing. It is a separate option and is documented as Public Preview for Model Serving.
## How passthrough works
At deployment Databricks verifies the endpoint creator can access each declared resource, creates a service principal for the agent model version, grants it read access to those resources, and injects short-lived M2M OAuth tokens it rotates. The behavior resembles "Run as owner" for dashboards.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Open to everyone:** this removes least privilege for every user and still does not give the endpoint a managed identity.
- ✗ **B. Personal token in a secret scope:** a long-lived credential tied to a person that must be rotated by hand; this is the manual route passthrough replaces.
- ✗ **C. Notebook only:** the requirement is a deployed endpoint; the notebook identity does not exist there.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Declared resources are exactly the input that automatic passthrough needs to give the endpoint short-lived, rotated credentials with least-privilege access.

## Key idea
Declare resources at logging time for automatic authentication passthrough.
Q012301:
## The creator's permissions matter
With automatic passthrough, Databricks first verifies that the endpoint creator can access every dependency declared at logging time, and then grants a created service principal access to them. So the person calling `deploy()` needs the permission for each resource type:
- Unity Catalog function: `EXECUTE`
- Unity Catalog table: `SELECT`
- AI Search index: `Can Use`
- Model Serving endpoint: `Can Query`
- Genie Agent: `Can Run`
- SQL warehouse: `Use Endpoint`
Unity Catalog resources also require `USE SCHEMA` on the parent schema and `USE CATALOG` on the parent catalog.
## Minimum fix
Grant exactly what the failing resource needs, no more.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Workspace admin:** it is far beyond the minimum fix and unnecessary for a single function.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** The function needs `EXECUTE`, and Unity Catalog objects also need `USE SCHEMA` and `USE CATALOG` on the parents, so granting those lets the creator pass the check.
- ✗ **C. CAN MANAGE on the index:** the index permission applies to the index, not to the function the error names.
- ✗ **D. CAN QUERY on the endpoint:** the endpoint is created by the deployment itself, and the failing check is about the function.

## Key idea
The deploying user needs each declared resource's permission, plus USE SCHEMA and USE CATALOG for UC objects.
Q012302:
## Permission by resource type
For automatic authentication passthrough the creator needs the following (Unity Catalog resources also need `USE SCHEMA` and `USE CATALOG` on the parents):
- SQL warehouse: `Use Endpoint`
- Model Serving endpoint: `Can Query`
- Unity Catalog function: `EXECUTE`
- Genie Agent: `Can Run`
- AI Search index: `Can Use`
- Unity Catalog table: `SELECT`
Each permission is the least privilege that allows the declared use.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Function with SELECT:** functions use `EXECUTE`; `SELECT` is for tables.
- ✗ **B. Warehouse with Can Manage:** the requirement is `Use Endpoint`, which is less than managing it.
- ✗ **C. Endpoint dependency with Can Manage:** a model serving endpoint needs `Can Query`.
- ✓ **D. AI Search index (correct):** `Can Use` is the documented permission for an AI Search index.
- ✓ **E. Genie Agent (correct):** `Can Run` is the documented permission for a Genie Agent resource.

## Key idea
Match each resource to its least-privilege permission, such as Can Run for Genie and Can Use for AI Search.
Q012303:
## Components of a simple RAG chain
A chain connects components in a fixed order, each consuming the previous one's output:
1. **Retriever**: finds relevant passages for the question (for example from a vector index).
2. **Prompt template**: merges the question and the retrieved context into the final prompt.
3. **Chat model**: generates the answer from that prompt.
4. **Output parser**: converts the model's message into the shape the caller needs, here a plain string.
In LangChain expression language this reads like `retriever | prompt | model | parser`. The question and the retrieved text both flow into the prompt before the model sees them.
## Source note
This is generic LangChain expression language (LCEL) behavior and is not described on the Databricks docs pages; it is not a Databricks-specific feature.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** The model can only use context that already sits in the prompt, so retrieval and prompt building come first, and parsing the answer comes last.
- ✗ **B. Model first:** the model would run without context or a prompt.
- ✗ **C. Parser first:** a parser works on a model's output, so it belongs at the end.
- ✗ **D. Model before retriever:** the retrieved passages would arrive after the answer has been generated.

## Key idea
A RAG chain runs retriever, prompt template, chat model, then output parser.
Q012304:
## Chain or agent
- A **chain** has a fixed sequence of steps decided by the developer. Behavior is predictable, latency is bounded and each step is easy to evaluate.
- An **agent** lets the model decide which tools to call and how many times, which suits tasks where the path is not known in advance. That flexibility costs extra model calls, variance and evaluation effort.
## Applying it
The billing flow is always the same, so there is nothing for the model to decide. A chain with a fixed lookup step, a prompt template and a model matches the requirement with the least complexity.
## Source note
This is generic LangChain expression language (LCEL) behavior and is not described on the Databricks docs pages; it is not a Databricks-specific feature.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Free tool-calling loop:** extra model calls and variance for a decision that never needs making.
- ✗ **B. Supervisor with workers:** multi-agent routing adds latency and complexity for a flow without branching.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** The path is fixed, so a simple chain gives bounded latency and predictable behavior and is easy to test.
- ✗ **D. Memorizing plans:** plan data changes and is private per customer, so a model cannot hold it reliably; the lookup returns current data.

## Key idea
Use a simple chain when the steps are fixed; use an agent when the model must choose the path.
Q012305:
## Input contract of a chain
The first component of a chain defines the keys it needs. A prompt template with `{context}` and `{question}` expects a mapping with exactly those keys. Invoking with `{"query": ...}` supplies neither, so rendering fails before the model is called.
## Repair
Place a mapping step in front of the prompt, for example a dictionary of runnables such as `{"context": retriever, "question": itemgetter("query")}`, so the retriever produces `context` and the incoming `query` becomes `question`. The error is raised while rendering the prompt, so model or parser settings are not involved.
## Source note
This is generic LangChain expression language (LCEL) behavior and is not described on the Databricks docs pages; it is not a Databricks-specific feature.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** The prompt needs `context` and `question`, so a mapping step must create them from the incoming input and the retriever.
- ✗ **B. Retry the parser:** the failure happens when the prompt is rendered, before any parsing, and the same input fails again.
- ✗ **C. JSON parser:** the parser is the last step and was never reached.
- ✗ **D. Temperature:** a sampling parameter of the model; it cannot supply variables for a template.

## Key idea
Match the chain's input keys to the prompt template variables, with a mapping step if needed.
Q012306:
## Output shaping in a chain
Chains end with an **output parser** that converts the model's message into the form the next system needs: plain text, JSON or a typed object. To get structured output, the prompt states the required format, and the parser validates and converts the response; many chat models also support structured-output or JSON mode, which can be bound to the model in the same chain.
## Why not push it downstream
Downstream regex extraction is brittle and spreads format knowledge across systems. The chain is the right place to enforce the contract, and it is a small change compared with training a model.
## Source note
This is generic LangChain expression language (LCEL) behavior and is not described on the Databricks docs pages; it is not a Databricks-specific feature.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Shorter output:** length does not make text valid JSON, and it can truncate the answer.
- ✗ **B. Fine-tune first:** heavy and slow for a requirement that a prompt and a parser can meet.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** A format instruction in the prompt plus a parsing step at the end of the chain makes the output contract explicit and fails early if the shape is wrong.
- ✗ **D. Regex downstream:** sentences change with every answer, so the extraction is brittle.

## Key idea
Enforce structured output inside the chain with a format instruction and an output parser.
Q012307:
## Model flavors
An MLflow model is a folder with the model files, the environment description and one or more **flavors**. A flavor tells MLflow how to save and load the object. Frameworks that MLflow knows, such as LangChain, have their own flavor (`mlflow.langchain`), and anything custom can be wrapped as a generic `python_function` (pyfunc) model.
## Code-based logging for chains
Databricks recommends Models from Code: the chain is written in a Python file that ends with `mlflow.models.set_model(chain)`, and `mlflow.langchain.log_model(lc_model="/path/to/agent.py", ...)` saves the file and the environment. When the model is loaded or served, the file is run to rebuild the chain, and a request calls `invoke`.
## Basic elements to decide at this step
The flavor, the chat and embedding models the chain calls, the retriever (for example an AI Search index), the package dependencies, an input example and a signature are the pieces that make a RAG chain loadable elsewhere.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Empty pyfunc class:** a pyfunc wrapper needs your own code to rebuild the chain, and the claim that only pyfunc can be reloaded is wrong because framework flavors have their own loaders.
- ✓ **B. LangChain flavor (correct):** it saves the chain code and environment, `mlflow.langchain.load_model` returns an object that supports `invoke`, and the same logged model can be served later.
- ✗ **C. sklearn flavor:** this flavor is written for scikit-learn estimators, so it does not know how to save or rebuild a LangChain chain with its retriever and prompt.
- ✗ **D. Pickled artifact:** a pickle is an untracked file with no flavor, environment or signature, and it cannot restore live connections to an index or a serving endpoint.

## Key idea
Log a LangChain chain with the LangChain flavor so MLflow can reload and serve it.
Q012308:
## Signatures for agents
A **model signature** describes the schema of a model's inputs and outputs, and tools such as AI Playground and the review app use it to know how to call the agent. For generic pyfunc code or a LangChain chain, you either define the signature yourself or give an `input_example` and let MLflow infer it.
## ResponsesAgent
`ResponsesAgent` is the interface Databricks recommends for authoring agents. Its input and output schema is fixed by the interface, so MLflow infers a valid signature for it at logging time and the signature step can be skipped.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Error without signature:** logging does not fail, because for this interface MLflow supplies the signature itself.
- ✗ **B. Input example required:** the interface already fixes the schema, so no input example is needed to enable the tools.
- ✗ **C. Schema ignored:** the logged signature is what lets tools validate requests and responses, and the interface supplies a valid one.
- ✓ **D. Automatic inference (correct):** the `ResponsesAgent` interface defines the request and response schema, so MLflow derives a valid signature at logging time and Playground and the review app can call the agent.

## Key idea
A ResponsesAgent gets its signature inferred, so no manual signature is needed.
Q012309:
## Signature and input example
A **model signature** describes the schema of a model's inputs and outputs. It lets MLflow validate calls and tells tools such as AI Playground and the review app how to talk to the model. You can define it by hand or let MLflow infer it from an **input example**, which must be a valid input to the chain.
## Agents
For agents written with `ResponsesAgent`, MLflow infers a signature automatically and you can skip this step. For LangChain chains and generic pyfunc code you provide either an explicit signature or an input example.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Signature inference (correct):** MLflow runs the example through the logging code and infers the signature, which downstream tools use to check that requests and responses have the right shape.
- ✗ **B. Bound to one question:** an example shows the input format and puts no limit on later questions or on which passages are retrieved.
- ✗ **C. Replaces resources:** the example says nothing about which index or endpoints are called; those are declared with the separate `resources` argument.
- ✗ **D. Cached answer:** the input example is only a sample of valid input and is not a cache, so every request still runs the chain.

## Key idea
An input example lets MLflow infer the signature that tools use to validate requests.
Q012310:
## Who embeds the query?
- **Delta Sync index with embeddings computed by Databricks**: the index knows the embedding endpoint, so a query can be plain `query_text`.
- **Delta Sync index with self-managed embeddings** (or a Direct Vector Access index): the index only holds vectors. The query must also be a vector, passed as `query_vector`.
## Same model on both sides
Similarity only has meaning if documents and queries are embedded by the same model with the same dimension. In a chain this is a retriever component: it first embeds the question with the indexing model, then calls `similarity_search`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. num_results:** how many results are requested has no effect on whether a query vector exists.
- ✗ **B. Hybrid:** hybrid adds keyword matching on top of vector search, but a self-managed index still needs a query vector for the vector part.
- ✗ **C. Scale to zero:** the index does not call any embedding endpoint in this setup, so changing the scaling of the chain's endpoint cannot help.
- ✓ **D. Query vector (correct):** a self-managed index has no embedding model attached, so the chain must embed the question with the same model used for the documents and pass `query_vector`.

## Key idea
With self-managed embeddings the chain embeds the query itself and sends `query_vector`.
Q012311:
## Models in Unity Catalog
Models registered in Unity Catalog are governed objects in the three-level namespace `<catalog>.<schema>.<model>`. Because of the namespace, the catalog or schema itself can express the environment (for example `dev`, `staging`, `prod`), and aliases mark the version to deploy. Stages are not supported in Unity Catalog. (The older workspace model registry is legacy.)
## Creating a registered model
- Set the registry with `mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")`.
- Pass the full three-level name to `registered_model_name` or `mlflow.register_model`.
- The principal needs `USE CATALOG` on the catalog, and `USE SCHEMA` and `CREATE MODEL` on the schema.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. models:/ prefix:** `models:/` is the form of a model URI used when loading a version, not the form of a registered model name.
- ✗ **B. Remove the registry setting:** the workspace registry is legacy, and it is the Unity Catalog registry that supports governance and agent deployment.
- ✓ **C. Three-level name (correct):** Unity Catalog needs a name of the form `catalog.schema.model` and the privileges to create a model in that schema.
- ✗ **D. Stage name:** stages are not supported in Unity Catalog, and versions are marked for deployment with aliases instead.

## Key idea
Register to Unity Catalog with a three-level name and the right privileges.
Q012312:
## Register an existing model
Logging and registering are separate steps. `log_model(..., registered_model_name=...)` does both at once, but a model that is already logged inside a run can be registered later with `mlflow.register_model(model_uri, name)`, where the URI has the form `runs:/<run_id>/<artifact_path>`. With the registry URI set to `databricks-uc`, the name must be the three-level name and each call creates a new version.
## Why it matters
The registered version points to the logged artifact that was reviewed, so what is evaluated is what is registered and later deployed.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Volume copy:** a volume is plain file storage, so copying files there creates no model version, no lineage and no signature check.
- ✓ **B. register_model (correct):** it takes the URI of the existing logged model and creates a version in the Unity Catalog model, so the reviewed artifact is the one registered.
- ✗ **C. Run tag:** tags are plain metadata on the run and do not register anything in Unity Catalog.
- ✗ **D. Log again:** logging again creates a different artifact in a new run, which is not the one that was reviewed.

## Key idea
Register an already logged run artifact with `mlflow.register_model` and a `runs:/` URI.
Q012313:
## Deploying a registered agent
`agents.deploy(uc_model_name, version)` takes a model registered in Unity Catalog, creates a Model Serving endpoint with automatic scaling and credentials for the declared resources, and integrates the endpoint with tracing and the review app.
## Updating a deployment
When you call `deploy()` with the same Unity Catalog model name as an existing deployment, the new model version is added to the existing endpoint. Traffic shifts after the new version is ready, and the previous version keeps serving during the rollout, so a version update does not interrupt callers and the endpoint URL stays the same.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Second endpoint:** the new version joins the existing endpoint, so clients keep the same URL and need no change.
- ✗ **B. Delete first:** the previous version continues to serve while the new one becomes ready, so the endpoint is not removed.
- ✓ **C. In-place update (correct):** a repeat deploy with the same model name updates the existing endpoint rather than replacing it, so callers keep one URL and see no downtime.
- ✗ **D. Only one version:** every new registered version can be deployed, since versions are exactly what Unity Catalog tracks for a model.

## Key idea
Deploying a new version of the same registered model updates the existing endpoint in place.
Q012314:
## Privileges for Unity Catalog models
A registered model is a securable object, a subtype of function, in a schema.
- **Create a registered model** needs `CREATE MODEL` and `USE SCHEMA` on the schema, plus `USE CATALOG`.
- **Create a new version** of an existing model needs ownership of the model, or `CREATE MODEL VERSION` on it, plus `USE SCHEMA` and `USE CATALOG`.
- **Use the model** (view it, load it) needs `EXECUTE` on the model plus the same catalog and schema usage.
## Why the difference matters
A team can let a CI service principal add versions to one governed model without letting it create other models in the schema.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. MANAGE on the catalog:** no catalog-wide control is needed, and granting it would be far broader than adding a version requires.
- ✗ **B. SELECT on the source table:** a model version is created from a logged artifact and not from table privileges.
- ✗ **C. CREATE MODEL on schema:** this privilege creates new registered models; versions of an existing model need ownership or the model-level privilege.
- ✓ **D. CREATE MODEL VERSION (correct):** adding a version to a model the user does not own needs this privilege on the registered model, together with usage of its schema and catalog.

## Key idea
A non-owner needs `CREATE MODEL VERSION` to add versions to a registered model.
Q012315:
## Creating an index with the SDK
The Python SDK (`databricks-ai-search`, class `AISearchClient`) creates indexes with `create_delta_sync_index` or `create_direct_access_index`. AI Search was called Mosaic AI Vector Search and Databricks Vector Search before; the exam guide and many API paths (`/vector-search/`) still use the old name.
## Choosing the arguments
- **Managed embeddings**: give `embedding_source_column` (the text column) and `embedding_model_endpoint_name` (the endpoint that computes embeddings).
- **Self-managed embeddings**: give `embedding_vector_column` (an array of floats) and `embedding_dimension`.
- `pipeline_type` is `TRIGGERED` (you start each sync) or `CONTINUOUS`.
- A Direct Vector Access index has no source table; you write rows with the SDK or REST API.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Triggered managed index (correct):** a text source column with an embedding model endpoint lets Databricks compute the vectors, and `TRIGGERED` refreshes the index only when the team starts a sync.
- ✗ **B. Direct access:** this index type has no source table and is updated by writing rows yourself, so it does not follow the Delta table.
- ✗ **C. Vector column arguments:** those describe pre-computed embeddings, but the `text` column holds strings and not arrays of floats.
- ✗ **D. Continuous with a vector column:** continuous sync updates on its own instead of on demand, and the column would again have to contain ready-made vectors.

## Key idea
Managed embeddings need a text column plus an embedding endpoint; triggered mode refreshes on demand.
Q012316:
## Which columns are available
By default all source columns are synced. With `columns_to_sync` only the listed columns (plus the primary key and the embedding column) are indexed. Only indexed columns can be returned in results or used as filters.
## Query filters
`similarity_search` accepts `filters` on any indexed column. On standard endpoints a filter is a dict such as `{"region": "EMEA"}` or `{"title NOT": "x"}`; storage-optimized endpoints use SQL-like strings.
## Schema changes
The index schema is fixed at creation. Changes to the source table, such as new or modified columns, require building a new index.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Larger num_results:** how many results are returned does not make an unsynced column filterable.
- ✓ **B. New index (correct):** `region` was not synced, so it can be neither filtered nor returned, and the index must be rebuilt with that column included.
- ✗ **C. Change source schema:** schema changes in the source are not picked up by an existing index, and a new index is needed.
- ✗ **D. NOT operator:** a different operator changes the match logic but still needs the column to be indexed.

## Key idea
Filters work only on indexed columns, and a missing column means a new index.
Q012317:
## Querying an index is governed by Unity Catalog
An AI Search index is a Unity Catalog object. A user or service principal that queries it needs `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` on its catalog and schema and `SELECT` on the index; the index owner has `SELECT` already. If Databricks computes the embeddings, the caller may also need permission on the embedding model endpoint. For production, Databricks recommends service principals.
## Creating vs querying
Creating an index is a different privilege: `CREATE TABLE` on the schema.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. SELECT on the index (correct):** reading nearest neighbors from the index is a select on the index object.
- ✗ **B. MODIFY on the source table:** the sync pipeline, not the querying principal, reads the source table, and MODIFY would allow writes the chain never performs.
- ✗ **C. MANAGE on the endpoint:** endpoint management is a separate access control list and querying an index does not require managing its endpoint.
- ✗ **D. CREATE TABLE:** this is the privilege needed to create an index, not to query one that exists.
- ✓ **E. Catalog and schema usage (correct):** the principal must be able to reach the index through its catalog and schema, which `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` allow.

## Key idea
Query access is `SELECT` on the index plus usage of its catalog and schema.
Q012318:
## Foundation Model APIs
Model Serving supports Foundation Model APIs: Databricks hosts foundation models, including open models, and exposes them as serving endpoints, so you build applications without maintaining your own model deployment. Pay-per-token endpoints are preconfigured in the workspace.
## Serving an application that uses them
The application you serve is the chain or agent. It calls the foundation model endpoint over the serving API. When you log it, you list the chat model endpoint and the index as `resources`; on deployment Model Serving gives the endpoint credentials for them. The chain is the only thing you deploy.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. External models only:** Foundation Model APIs endpoints can be called from applications and chains, not only from notebooks.
- ✓ **B. Deploy only the chain (correct):** Foundation Model APIs endpoints are already hosted, so the chain is deployed with the model endpoint and the index declared as resources.
- ✗ **C. Copy weights:** the chain calls the hosted endpoint over the serving API and does not embed model weights.
- ✗ **D. Create provisioned throughput first:** provisioned throughput is an option for guaranteed capacity, not a requirement for calling a hosted model from a chain.

## Key idea
Deploy the chain and declare the Foundation Model APIs endpoint as a resource.
Q012319:
## Foundation Model APIs modes
- **Pay-per-token**: preconfigured endpoints for supported models, the easiest way to start. Standard requests are best-effort, so latency can vary under load.
- **Priority pay-per-token**: an opt-in per request (`service_tier` set to `"priority"`) for latency-sensitive, real-time applications. It admits the request ahead of standard traffic, needs no commitment and is billed at a higher per-token rate.
- **Provisioned throughput**: dedicated capacity for high throughput, performance guarantees or fine-tuned models, as on-demand or reserved (fixed term).
- **AI Functions optimized models**: meant for batch inference with AI Functions.
## Choosing
Consistent latency with per-token billing and no commitment points to priority mode; guaranteed capacity or a fine-tuned model points to provisioned throughput.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Larger max_tokens:** the output limit is a request setting that does not change how the request is scheduled.
- ✗ **B. AI Functions optimized:** this mode is recommended for batch inference, not for interactive chat.
- ✗ **C. Reserved provisioned throughput:** it gives dedicated capacity but needs a fixed-term commitment and capacity planning, which the team cannot accept, and a per-token option for steadier latency exists.
- ✓ **D. Priority mode (correct):** the `service_tier` parameter set to `"priority"` gets requests admitted ahead of standard traffic for more consistent latency, with no commitment and per-token billing.

## Key idea
Priority pay-per-token adds consistent latency without a commitment.
Q012320:
## OpenAI-compatible querying
Model Serving uses a unified OpenAI-compatible API and SDK for Foundation Model APIs and external models. Options for querying include the OpenAI client, the REST API (`POST /serving-endpoints/{name}/invocations`), the MLflow Deployments SDK, the Foundation Models Python SDK and the UI. Databricks recommends the OpenAI client for extended interactions with compatible models. Requests need a Databricks API token.
## Using the client
Install `databricks-openai` for a client with authorization configured, or point the standard client at the workspace; the endpoint name is the `model` argument.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. JDBC:** serving endpoints are not exposed as tables of a SQL warehouse, so there is nothing to query that way.
- ✗ **B. ai_query:** this is a SQL function for SQL and batch use, and it is not needed because the client library can query endpoints directly.
- ✓ **C. OpenAI client (correct):** the OpenAI-compatible API lets existing client code work against a Databricks endpoint with a token and the endpoint name as `model`.
- ✗ **D. ONNX export:** the endpoints do accept OpenAI-style requests and the model is already hosted, so running it locally is unnecessary work.

## Key idea
Existing OpenAI client code can call Foundation Model APIs with a Databricks token and the endpoint name.
Q012321:
## Components
- **Source table**: a Delta table, streaming table, materialized view or managed Iceberg table that holds the text or the vectors.
- **Index**: stores the embedded data with metadata. It appears in and is governed by Unity Catalog, so privileges apply.
- **Endpoint**: the compute that serves queries for indexes. One endpoint can host several indexes, and endpoints scale automatically with the size of the indexes and the number of concurrent requests.
- **Embedding model**: a Foundation Model APIs or custom serving endpoint, used when Databricks computes the embeddings.
## Name
Mosaic AI Vector Search became Databricks AI Search; APIs still say `vector-search`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Serving endpoint as store:** an embedding endpoint computes vectors for the index, but the index is what stores them.
- ✗ **B. Index per query:** indexes are created once and queried many times, and an endpoint does not hold the source text.
- ✗ **C. Volume and notebook:** the index stores the vectors, and a notebook is not the serving layer for queries.
- ✓ **D. Source table, index, endpoint (correct):** the source table feeds the index, the index is a Unity Catalog object with its own privileges, and an endpoint serves one or more indexes.

## Key idea
A source table feeds a governed index that an endpoint serves.
Q012322:
## Two index types
- **Delta Sync index**: follows a source table and updates incrementally when the table changes. Embeddings can be computed by Databricks (from a text column) or supplied by you (a vector column).
- **Direct Vector Access index**: supports direct read and write of vectors and metadata. You update it with the REST API or the Python SDK (`index.upsert`); it cannot be created in the UI.
## Choosing
If a Delta table is the source of truth, use Delta Sync. If an application manages the vectors itself, use Direct Vector Access.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Delta Sync with managed embeddings:** it is fed from a source table and is not updated by API upserts.
- ✗ **B. Continuous sync:** continuous mode follows changes in the source table and does not accept rows inserted by the application.
- ✓ **C. Direct Vector Access (correct):** it has no source table, and the application updates it through the SDK or REST API with upserts and deletes.
- ✗ **D. Full-text index:** the dedicated full-text index holds no embeddings, so it is not the right index for vectors.

## Key idea
No source table and API-managed vectors means Direct Vector Access.
Q012323:
## Approximate nearest neighbors
AI Search uses the Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) algorithm for approximate nearest neighbor search and the L2 distance to measure similarity. With normalized vectors, the ranking by L2 equals the ranking by cosine similarity, so to get cosine behavior you normalize the embeddings first.
## Hybrid search
Hybrid keyword-similarity search combines this vector search with keyword search (BM25) and merges the rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which helps for exact identifiers such as SKUs.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. BM25 only:** BM25 is the keyword part of hybrid search, while plain queries rank by vector similarity.
- ✓ **B. L2 and normalization (correct):** the metric is L2, and normalized vectors make the L2 ranking the same as a cosine ranking.
- ✗ **C. Exact scan:** the search is approximate by design, trading a little recall for speed on large indexes.
- ✗ **D. Cosine default:** L2 is the metric used, which is exactly why normalization matters for cosine behavior.
- ✓ **E. HNSW (correct):** the index is searched approximately with the HNSW graph algorithm instead of an exact scan.

## Key idea
AI Search is HNSW with L2; normalize for cosine.
Q012324:
## The request argument
`ai_query(endpoint, request, ...)` queries a Databricks foundation model endpoint, an external model endpoint or a custom model endpoint in the same workspace. What `request` may be depends on the endpoint type.
- Foundation Model APIs and external model endpoints: a `STRING`.
- Custom model endpoints: a single column or a `STRUCT` expression whose field names match the input feature names that the endpoint expects.
## Related arguments
`returnType`, `failOnError`, `modelParameters` and `responseFormat` (for chat models) shape the result; the definer needs `CAN QUERY` on the endpoint.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. STRUCT request (correct):** a custom model endpoint takes a `STRUCT` whose field names equal its input features, so `named_struct` maps the `months` column to `tenure`.
- ✗ **B. Concatenated string:** a custom model expects structured inputs by feature name, not a prompt string.
- ✗ **C. Multiple arguments:** the function takes one request expression, so features must be packed into one struct.
- ✗ **D. Single column:** names are matched to features, and the function does not rename a column to the first feature.

## Key idea
For custom endpoints pass a column or a STRUCT with the feature names.
Q012325:
## Batch inference as a pipeline
Batch inference applies a model to many rows and writes the result to a table, with no one waiting on individual answers. Databricks documents pipelines that combine ingestion, preprocessing, inference and post-processing and are deployed as Lakeflow pipelines, scheduled jobs or Structured Streaming jobs.
## The incremental pattern
Ingest into a streaming table with `read_files`, apply `ai_query` (with `responseFormat` to force a JSON schema), and add `EXPECT` constraints in a downstream step to validate labels before later steps. Because ingestion is incremental, previously loaded files are not read again.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Rereading the archive:** this reprocesses old tickets every hour and pays for the model calls again.
- ✗ **B. Endpoint loop:** this is real-time style calling for a batch task, with no scheduling, incremental ingestion or output validation.
- ✓ **C. Incremental pipeline (correct):** a Lakeflow pipeline ingests only new files, applies `ai_query` in bulk, and expectations validate the labels before they are used.
- ✗ **D. Dashboard filter:** inference would run on every view instead of once per ticket, and nothing is written to a table.

## Key idea
Use an incremental pipeline with ai_query for continuous batch inference.

## Where AI Functions run
AI Functions, including `ai_query`, are not available on Classic SQL warehouses. They run from Databricks SQL on serverless warehouses, from notebooks and clusters (with a supported Databricks Runtime), from Lakeflow pipelines and from jobs. When you call one, the query runs on the compute you submit it from, and the model inference may run on separate Databricks-managed infrastructure billed in addition.
## Related requirements
The caller also needs query permission on the endpoint and on the Delta table.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Supported compute (correct):** the restriction is on the compute type, so the fix is to run the same call on serverless SQL, a notebook, a cluster or a pipeline.
- ✗ **B. Streaming table:** AI Functions work on batch tables too, so the source type is not the issue.
- ✗ **C. try_cast:** a cast only changes a value type and cannot make an unsupported compute type run the function.
- ✗ **D. Bigger warehouse:** size does not change which compute types support AI Functions.

## Key idea
Run ai_query on serverless or runtime compute, not on a classic warehouse.
Q012327:
## Endpoint types
- **Standard**: lower query latency, supports continuous and triggered sync and high QPS scaling for sustained throughput.
- **Storage-optimized**: a much larger capacity, faster indexing and a price tuned for very large vector counts, with slightly higher query latency. Only triggered sync is supported.
## Sizing
Each endpoint scales up automatically to the size of its indexes. A standard unit covers fewer vectors than a storage-optimized unit.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. High target QPS:** it provisions extra capacity for throughput and raises cost, but it does not add storage capacity per unit.
- ✗ **B. Continuous sync:** this setting affects freshness of the index, not how fast a very large index is built.
- ✗ **C. Many direct-access indexes:** splitting across standard endpoints complicates queries and costs more for this size.
- ✓ **D. Storage-optimized (correct):** this endpoint type is designed for very large indexes with fast indexing and a lower cost per vector, at a small latency penalty.

## Key idea
Huge, often rebuilt indexes with relaxed latency use storage-optimized endpoints.
Q012328:
## Sync modes
- **Continuous**: the index follows the source with latency of seconds, using a provisioned streaming pipeline, so it costs more.
- **Triggered**: you start the sync with the SDK, REST API or UI; it is the cheapest option.
## Endpoint limit
Storage-optimized endpoints support only Triggered sync, and each sync partially rebuilds the index. Standard endpoints support both modes, with incremental updates.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Continuous on storage-optimized:** this combination is not supported because only triggered sync is available there.
- ✓ **B. Standard with continuous sync (correct):** seconds-level freshness needs continuous sync, and only standard endpoints support it.
- ✗ **C. Direct access:** the application would have to upsert every changed row itself, which is code, and it changes the design.
- ✗ **D. Scheduled sync:** a periodic sync is minute-level at best, and each run partially rebuilds a storage-optimized index.

## Key idea
Seconds-level freshness means continuous sync on a standard endpoint.
Q012329:
## Cost drivers
AI Search bills for indexes (stored vectors) and endpoints (serving queries). Each endpoint has a base price and scales with the indexes it serves, and one endpoint can host many indexes.
## Practices
- Combine small, low-QPS workloads on one endpoint to avoid multiple base costs.
- Use Triggered sync instead of Continuous sync where possible, because continuous sync provisions a streaming cluster.
- Find endpoints with no traffic using audit logs; they still incur serving costs.
- A target QPS adds capacity that is charged regardless of traffic.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. High target QPS:** it adds capacity that is paid for regardless of actual traffic, so it raises cost.
- ✗ **B. Continuous everywhere:** it provisions a streaming cluster per index and costs more than triggered syncs.
- ✓ **C. Shared endpoint (correct):** one base cost replaces eight, and small low-QPS indexes fit on one endpoint.
- ✗ **D. Idle endpoints:** endpoints whose indexes get no queries still incur serving costs.
- ✓ **E. Triggered sync (correct):** no always-on streaming pipeline is needed when second-level freshness is not a requirement.

## Key idea
Share endpoints and use triggered sync to cut AI Search cost.
Q012330:
## Two kinds of agent state
Databricks offers managed stores for both kinds, backed by Lakebase (managed Postgres) and usable with any agent framework.
- **Agent sessions**: state for one interaction, most often the conversation history with tool calls, so an interaction survives restarts.
- **Agent memory**: durable facts, preferences and decisions recalled by semantic search in later, separate conversations.
Use both together for most use cases. The earlier managed memory store governed by Unity Catalog is legacy.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Single Delta table:** reading the whole table every turn does not scale and gives no semantic recall of durable facts.
- ✗ **B. Local list:** a file written at shutdown is lost on a crash and is not shared across agent instances.
- ✗ **C. Search index only:** raw chat logs mix transcript with durable facts, and an index has no notion of a resumable session.
- ✓ **D. Sessions and memory (correct):** sessions give continuity within a conversation and memory gives it across conversations, both stored durably in Lakebase.

## Key idea
Sessions hold one interaction; memory holds durable cross-conversation facts.
Q012331:
## Transactional state
Lakebase is a fully managed Postgres database integrated into Databricks. It is meant for low-latency transactional applications and can serve as a state store for agents, with Unity Catalog integration and autoscaling.
## Other stores
Delta tables are for analytics and batch pipelines, AI Search indexes for retrieval, and volumes for files.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Volume files:** files have no transactions, and reading one file per task is slow for lookups.
- ✓ **B. Lakebase (correct):** frequent row-level updates with millisecond reads are a transactional pattern, which a managed Postgres database serves.
- ✗ **C. Search index:** it is built for similarity retrieval and not for transactional state updates.
- ✗ **D. Nightly Delta rewrite:** the task state would be hours old, which defeats frequent updates read back within milliseconds.

## Key idea
Use Lakebase for agent state needing transactional low-latency updates.
Q012332:
## Memory pipelines
A memory pipeline reads conversations in a session store, extracts durable facts and writes them to a memory store, so memory builds without memory-writing tools in the agent.
## Independence of the stores
Memory is scoped to a subject, not to an interaction. Deleting a session, or an entire session store, does not delete memory retained in a memory store.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Memory pipeline (correct):** it distills sessions into memory on demand or on a schedule, and the memories remain after the sessions are cleared.
- ✗ **B. Copy transcripts:** raw transcripts are not distilled facts, so the memory store would just duplicate the session store.
- ✗ **C. Agent tool:** this works but it is exactly the memory-writing tool the team wants to avoid, and pipelines can read the session store.
- ✗ **D. Expiry deletes memory:** the stores are independent, so clearing sessions does not remove memories.

## Key idea
Memory pipelines turn sessions into durable memory.
Q012333:
## Keeping the index current
A Triggered Delta Sync index updates only when you start a sync with the SDK, REST API or UI; Continuous indexes update automatically. In automation, add a job task after the source-table task that calls the sync. Upserts apply to Direct Vector Access indexes.
## Schema changes
New or changed source columns require a new index.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Self-updating:** a Triggered index never syncs by itself, so the content stays old until a sync is started.
- ✓ **B. Sync task (correct):** starting a sync after the table refresh makes the index pick up only the changed rows, so a job task closes the gap.
- ✗ **C. Recreate every run:** a full rebuild recomputes embeddings and costs more than an incremental sync.
- ✗ **D. Upsert:** this API writes to Direct Vector Access indexes and is not used on a Delta Sync index.

## Key idea
Add a sync step to the job after refreshing the source table.
Q012334:
## Promotion across environments
Databricks recommends deploying code, so that production models are produced by automated workflows in the production environment. When retraining or relogging in each environment is too expensive, you can copy model versions across registered models in Unity Catalog.
## How it works
The catalog expresses the environment. `copy_model_version(src_uri, dst_name)` copies the version, privileges on both models decide who may promote, and an alias such as `Champion` marks the version to deploy after validation. Stages are not supported.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Stages:** stages are not supported for Unity Catalog models, which use aliases and catalogs.
- ✗ **B. Rename the model:** renaming does not move it between catalogs and would remove the staging copy used for testing.
- ✓ **C. Copy then alias (correct):** `copy_model_version` creates the version in the production model, and an alias marks it for deployment once validated.
- ✗ **D. Wheel export:** a wheel is a package format and not a model promotion path with governance and lineage.

## Key idea
Copy the version across catalogs, then mark it with an alias.
Q012335:
## Deploy code vs deploy models
- **Deploy code (recommended)**: code for training or agent logging moves through dev, staging and prod; the production model is produced by a run in production, and tests run in each environment.
- **Deploy models**: a model artifact is built in dev and promoted; this is the alternative pattern.
## Testing agent components
Unit tests cover single pieces such as tool functions or retrieval logic, integration tests exercise the chain with real endpoints in staging, and CI/CD runs them before release.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Deploy code (correct):** the recommended pattern promotes code through the environments, with unit tests on components and integration tests in staging.
- ✗ **B. Prod only:** manual tests in prod are risky and not repeatable, unlike automated CI tests in staging.
- ✗ **C. Skip pre-production:** relying on user feedback in prod exposes users to defects that tests would catch.
- ✗ **D. Model artifact only:** promoting the artifact is the deploy-models pattern, which is the alternative and skips testing in later environments.

## Key idea
Deploy code and test components in CI before prod.
